title: Classical continua with explicit constitutive assumptions

items.title: Continuum body data, the fixed inertial frame and the dimensions of the fields
items.design_state: authored; step-1 readiness recorded in the batch notes
items.physical_scope: The kinematic and dimensional framework of the continuum branch: one fixed inertial frame, a reference material region with a reference chart domain, a time window, and the dimensions of the density, velocity, acceleration, body-force, traction, stress, displacement, elastic, viscous, pressure and wave-speed fields. The definition fixes conventions only; it asserts no motion, no balance law, no constitutive relation and no measured value.

references.title: R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Sections 1.2-1.6 (continuous bodies, reference and current configurations) and Section 3.1 (motion and velocity)

K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (September 1, 2026 complete volume), Section 7.1 (the continuum approximation and deformations) and Section 8.3 (the velocity field of a continuum)

items.statement:
**(a) Framework and frame.** The framework is the non-relativistic classical
mechanics of [[post-cm01-spacetime]] with the inertial frames, stationary
observers and allowed changes of frame of [[post-cm01-frames]]; the particle
worldline conventions of [[post-cm01-worldlines]] are used for the labeled
points of a body, and dimensions and reference units (metre, second, kilogram)
are read by [[def-cm01-units]]. Throughout this page one inertial frame $F$
with adapted coordinates $(t,x)$ of the affine time space
[[def-cm-affine-time-space]] is fixed, and each simultaneous spatial slice is
identified with $\mathbb R^3$ carrying its standard Euclidean structure. The
time coordinate $t$ is the model's time in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the
spatial components $x_i$ are positions in metres, $[x_i]=\ell$. All fields
below are read in this one frame.

**(b) Body data.** A **continuum body data set** in $F$ is a triple $(B,O,I)$
consisting of

1. a material region $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$: a nonempty, bounded, open set
   ([[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]);
2. an open set $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with $\overline B\subseteq O$, the
   **reference chart domain**;
3. a nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$, the **time window**
   ([[def-interval]]).

The points $X\in B$ are the **material labels** of the body and $B$ is its
**reference placement**. The reference placement is bookkeeping for the
labels and not an observable: it is used only to name the points of the body,
and all physical statements of this page concern spatial fields on the
current regions and their transformation between frames. The label set
carries no metric, mass or force of its own.

**(c) Field slots and dimensions.** The following fields are attached to body
data of this branch; each dimension is computed from the stated defining
relation with the rules of [[def-cm01-units]], and every display of this page
must be dimensionally consistent:

1. **density** $\rho$, mass per unit volume, $[\rho]=\mu\ell^{-3}$;
2. **spatial velocity** $u$, $[u]=\ell\tau^{-1}$, and **material
   acceleration** $a=D_tu$, $[a]=\ell\tau^{-2}$;
3. **body force per unit mass** $b$, an acceleration, $[b]=\ell\tau^{-2}$;
   the corresponding force per volume is $\rho b$ of dimension
   $\mu\ell^{-2}\tau^{-2}$;
4. **traction** $t$ and **stress matrix** $\sigma$, force per unit area,
   $[t]=[\sigma]=\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-2}$ (in SI, $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$);
5. **displacement** $\xi$, $[\xi]=\ell$; **linear strain** $e$, dimensionless;
6. **elastic moduli** $\lambda,\mu_s$ and **pressure** $p$ of dimension
   $\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-2}$; **dynamic viscosity** $\eta$ of dimension
   $\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-1}$ (SI, $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$);
7. **wave speed** $c$, $[c]=\ell\tau^{-1}$, and **enthalpy per unit mass**
   $h$, $[h]=\ell^2\tau^{-2}$.

**(d) Frame and reference-label conventions.** Write a Galilean change as
$$G(t,x)=(t',x')=(t+\beta,Rx+vt+a_0),\qquad R\in SO(3),$$
with the conventions of [[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]]. At corresponding events, a scalar field $q$ (density $\rho$, pressure $p$ or enthalpy $h$) transforms by $q'\circ G=q$. Spatial vectors such as acceleration and force per unit mass transform by $a'\circ G=Ra$, $b'\circ G=Rb$, while velocity has the boost term $u'\circ G=Ru+v$. Normals transform by $n'=Rn$, traction by
$$t'(G(t,x),Rn)=R\,t(t,x,n),$$
and stress by $\sigma'\circ G=R\sigma R^{\mathsf T}$. Rotations preserve spatial volume and area. Spatial differentiation is at fixed frame time; these rules give $D_{x'}u'=R(D_xu)R^{\mathsf T}$, $\operatorname{div}_{x'}u'=\operatorname{div}_xu$ and $D_{t'}u'=R D_tu$ at corresponding events. Thus $t=\sigma n$ and the local mass and momentum equations have the same form, as do their volume and surface integral forms.

For a reference-label chart choose a fixed reference time $t_{\mathrm r}\in I$ and set $X'=RX+vt_{\mathrm r}+a_0$. This is a time-independent relabeling, with $B',O'$ the images of $B,O$, and
$$\chi'(t',X')=R\chi(t,X)+vt+a_0,\qquad t=t'-\beta.$$
A material scalar transforms by composition with the inverse label/time map; a material vector by that composition followed by $R$. In the linear elastic branch the stress-free comparison placement $X$ in $F$ transforms to the uniformly translating comparison placement $RX+vt+a_0$ in $F'$. Define displacement as the difference from this same comparison placement, so
$$\xi'(t',X')=R\xi(t,X),\qquad D_{X'}\xi'=R(D_X\xi)R^{\mathsf T},\qquad e'=ReR^{\mathsf T}.$$
Time derivatives here are at fixed labels. Consequently $\partial_{t'}^2\xi'=R\partial_t^2\xi$, while spatial velocity in the boosted description is $v+R\partial_t\xi$. The convention $u=\partial_t\xi$ applies in the chosen frame where the comparison placement is stationary. Constant isotropic elastic moduli and viscosity are scalars; the isotropic strain-stress law is carried to the same law by these rules. These are coordinate-reading rules, not a finite-strain approximation theorem or a new constitutive assumption.

items.title: Adopted continuum kinematic model: body data, smooth motions as families of label worldlines, the continuum idealization and frame covariance
items.design_state: authored; step-1 readiness recorded in the batch notes
items.physical_scope: Adoption of the kinematic branch of the continuum framework: every model is carried by body data in a fixed inertial frame; the body's motion is a C^2 family of orientation-preserving injective configurations whose labels follow worldlines and whose velocity field carries the model's spatial velocity and material acceleration; the continuum hypothesis, the smoothness idealization and the frame-covariance requirement are stated. The postulate excludes fracture, interpenetration, phase boundaries, shocks, diffusion, chemical reactions and thermal or electromagnetic coupling, and asserts no dynamics, no constitutive relation and no measured value.

references.title: R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Sections 1.2-1.6 (continuous bodies and motions) and 3.1-3.3 (velocity, velocity gradient)
K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (September 1, 2026 complete volume), Sections 7.1 and 8.3 (continuum description, particle displacement and velocity field)
I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09/8.309 Fall 2014 course text), Section 6.1 (the continuum description of a chain and the displacement field)

items.statement:
Adopt as physical assumptions of the continuum branch the following statements,
in the framework, frame and body data of [[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]].

**(i) Model data.** A model of the branch is carried by a continuum body data
set $(B,O,I)$ of [[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]] in the fixed inertial
frame $F$: a material region $B$, a reference chart domain $O$ with
$\overline B\subseteq O$, and a time window $I$. The labels $X\in B$ are the
material points of the body.

**(ii) Motion.** A **motion** of the model is a map

$$\chi:I\times O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3$$

which is a motion of the material region $B$ on $I$ in the sense of
[[def-cm-continuum-motion]]: $\chi$ is of class $C^2$; for every $t\in I$ the
map $\chi_t:O\to\mathbb R^3$ is of class $C^1$, injective and has invertible
total derivative at every point of $O$; and the Jacobian
$J(t,X)=\det\bigl(D_X\chi_t(X)\bigr)$ satisfies $J>0$ on $I\times B$. The
current region is $\Omega_t:=\chi_t(B)$, and the model's **spatial velocity
field** $u$ and **material acceleration** $a=D_tu$ are those of
[[def-cm-continuum-motion]] and [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]].

**(iii) Worldlines of labels.** For every label $X\in B$ the curve
$\gamma_X:I\to A$, $\gamma_X(t):=(t,\chi(t,X))$, is a worldline of the model in
the sense of clauses (i)-(iv) of [[post-cm01-worldlines]]: it is of class
$C^2$ in the adapted coordinates of $F$, its parameter is the frame time
($\tau(\gamma_X(t)-o)=t$), its description in another inertial frame is the
reparametrized curve induced by the frame change, and its coordinate velocity
and acceleration are read by [[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]. The motion is
thus a family of worldlines, one for each label, and the spatial velocity
field satisfies $u(t,\chi(t,X))=\partial_t\chi(t,X)$; no mass is attached to a
label, mass entering only through a density field.

**(iv) Continuum idealization.** The body is described as a continuum: every
label is a point and the fields are defined at every point of the current
regions. The following are **excluded** by this postulate, and no statement of
this page covers them: fracture, cutting or interpenetration (injectivity and
$J>0$); shocks, phase boundaries and material interfaces inside the motion
(the motion is $C^2$ with $J>0$ everywhere on $I\times B$); diffusion or
exchange of material between labels; chemical reactions, phase change and
mass sources; electromagnetic, thermal and radiative couplings; and
microscopic or molecular structure. The smoothness classes of the fields are
stated in each later item; wherever a weaker regularity is required it is
stated there, and the classical transport and balance identities of this page
are used only under their own hypotheses.

**(v) Frame covariance.** A model is **frame-covariant** when, for every
change of inertial frame $F\to F'$ given by the Galilean transformation of
[[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]], the description of the same motion in $F'$
is the Galilean transform of the description in $F$, and the model's balance
and constitutive laws have the same form when written in $F'$ with the
correspondingly transformed fields (velocities transformed by the boost,
accelerations rotated as there stated). The branch **requires** frame
covariance of every model; for each law adopted below, the covariance check
is carried out or the law is stated only in the fixed frame.

**(vi) Status.** These are adopted assumptions of the model. They are not
derived from mechanics and they assert nothing about any particular material.
The continuum idealization is used in practice when the fields vary on
spatial scales large compared with the microscopic spacing of the material
and the material admits a representative volume element; those microscopic
conditions are not formalized here and no quantitative threshold is
asserted. Empirical adequacy of the idealization for a given material is a
matter of comparison with observations and is not established by this
postulate.

items.title: The density field of the continuum model and the mass of a material subregion
items.design_state: authored; step-1 readiness recorded in the batch notes
items.physical_scope: The density field of a continuum model, its dimensions (mass per unit volume), and the model's mass of a material subregion at a given time, computed as the Lebesgue integral of the density over the current image of the subregion. The definition distinguishes the model field and its integral from any measured mass; it asserts no conservation, no positivity law of nature and no empirical value.

references.title: R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Sections 1.8 (extensive properties and their densities) and 4.2 (mass and its conservation)
K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (September 1, 2026 complete volume), Sections 7.1 and 8.3 (continuous medium, density and velocity fields)

items.statement:
Fix body data $(B,O,I)$ and a motion $\chi$ of the model on $I$ in the sense
of [[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]]; write $\Omega_t=\chi_t(B)$ for the
current regions and, for an open interval $J_0$ with $\overline{J_0}\subseteq
I$, let $\Sigma=\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\ x\in\chi_t(\overline B)\}$ be the
swept region ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]]).

A **density field of the model** is a function

$$\rho:U\longrightarrow(0,\infty)$$

on an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ containing the full swept set $\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(\overline B)\}$ (and hence $\Sigma$ for every compactly contained $J_0$),
whose physical reading is mass per unit volume: its dimension is
$[\rho]=\mu\ell^{-3}$ ([[def-cm01-units]], [[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]]).
The **standing regularity** of the balance items of this page is that $\rho$
is of class $C^1$ on $U$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]);
where a weaker regularity is used it is stated in the item that uses it.
Strict positivity and $C^1$ regularity are part of the field class of this
branch; the mathematical material-region notion that underlies it admits any
nonnegative integrable density ([[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]) and is
used here only to define the mass integral.

A **material subregion** at the level of labels is a nonempty bounded open
$B'\subseteq B$ with $\overline{B'}\subseteq B$
([[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]); the same $\chi$ is a motion of
$B'$. For the Lebesgue mass construction assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as in the density/mass part of [[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]; the positive $C^1$ field slot and the open-region predicate themselves require no choice axiom. For $t\in I$ the **model mass of $B'$ at time $t$** is the Lebesgue
integral

$$m(t,B'):=\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho(t,x)\,dx$$

([[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]]). Its dimension is $\mu$ and it is a
number computed from the model fields; whether it equals a measured mass is
not asserted here, and a comparison with an observed mass requires an
explicit measurement model, calibration and uncertainty statements that are
not part of this definition.

items.title: Adopted mass balance: the mass of every material subregion is constant in time
items.design_state: authored; step-1 readiness recorded in the batch notes
items.physical_scope: Adoption of mass conservation for a closed continuum model: for every material subregion and every time in the window, the model mass integral over the current image of the subregion is constant. The postulate excludes open systems, diffusion or exchange of material between labels, chemical reactions, phase change and mass sources; it asserts no empirical law and no measured value, and the local continuity equation is a theorem conditional on it.

references.title: R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Section 4.2 (the principle of conservation of mass and its local form)
K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (September 1, 2026 complete volume), Section 8.3 (continuity equation of a continuum)

items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the general Lebesgue mass integrals of [[def-cm17-density-and-mass]]; this qualifies the mathematical mass construction, not the choice-free kinematics.

Adopt the following assumption for every model of the continuum kinematic
branch of [[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]] with density field of
[[def-cm17-density-and-mass]].

**(i) Mass balance.** Let $\chi$ be a motion of the model on the time window
$I$, let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with $\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$,
and let $B'\subseteq B$ be a material subregion (nonempty bounded open with
$\overline{B'}\subseteq B$). Then the model mass of $B'$,

$$m(t,B')=\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho(t,x)\,dx\qquad(t\in J_0),$$

is constant in $t$:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho(t,x)\,dx=0\qquad(t\in J_0). \tag{CM}$$

The assumption is imposed for **every** material subregion and every time in
the window; the family of subregions is not restricted to a selected finite
list.

**(ii) Reading and exclusions.** The assumption says that a label carries its
matter permanently: the material of the body is a closed mechanical system
during the motion. It is **not** adopted, and no statement of this page
covers: open systems in which material is added to or removed from the body;
diffusion, mixing or relative transport of distinct constituents between
labels; chemical reactions, phase change or mass exchange between
constituents; mass sources or sinks distributed in the body; and relativistic
mass-energy conversion. In such situations the balance above can fail and a
different balance with source terms is required.

**(iii) Empirical status.** The assumption is the classical conservation of
mass, adopted here as model structure. Comparisons of predictions with
observed masses of prepared closed systems can support it under stated
apparatus and calibration assumptions; such comparisons are evidence about
the combined model and apparatus, not a deductive proof of the principle, and
no measurement is asserted or used by this postulate.

**(iv) Status of the consequences.** The local continuity equation derived on
this page is a conditional theorem: it follows from (CM) together with the
declared regularity of the fields and the transport identity of the kinematic
branch. If (CM) is replaced by a balance with sources, the local equation
acquires the corresponding source terms and none of the present deductions
applies unchanged.

items.title: The transport identity and the material derivative along label worldlines for the adopted continuum model
items.design_state: authored; step-1 readiness recorded in the batch notes
items.physical_scope: Conditional on the adopted continuum kinematic model (smooth motion with positive Jacobian) and on the Axiom of Countable Choice used by the cited change-of-variables theorem: for a C^1 spatial field on a neighbourhood of the swept region of a body over a compactly contained time interval, the rate of change of the field's integral over the current image of the body equals the integral of the local time derivative plus the flux term div(fu); and along the worldline of a label the ordinary time derivative of the material field equals the material derivative D_tf = partial_t f + grad f . u. The theorem asserts no balance law and no empirical value.

references.title: R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Sections 3.7 (transport equations) and 1.4-1.6 (material and spatial descriptions, material derivative)

W. Barsukow, Introduction to Conservation Laws: Theory and Numerics (lecture notes, TUM, Winter term 2021/22), Section 1.2.3, Theorem 1.1 (the transport theorem) and Section 1.1 (the advective derivative)

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the transport theorem cited below. Let
$(B,O,I)$ be body data of [[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]], let $\chi$ be
a motion of the model on $I$ with spatial velocity $u$ and material
acceleration $a=D_tu$ ([[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]],
[[def-cm-continuum-motion]]). Let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with
$\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$, put $\Sigma:=\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\
x\in\chi_t(\overline B)\}$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^1$ on an
open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ containing $\Sigma$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Then:

**(i) Transport identity.** The function $F(t):=\int_{\chi_t(B)}f(t,x)\,dx$ is
defined and differentiable on $J_0$, and for every $t\in J_0$

$$F'(t)=\int_{\chi_t(B)}\bigl(\partial_tf+\operatorname{div}(fu)\bigr)(t,x)\,dx .$$

The identity holds componentwise for a $C^1$ vector field $f$.

**(ii) Material derivative along worldlines.** If $f$ is the spatial
description of a material field $F_{\mathrm m}(t,X):=f(t,\chi(t,X))$, then for
every $X\in B$ the function $t\mapsto F_{\mathrm m}(t,X)$ is differentiable on
$J_0$ and

$$\frac{d}{dt}F_{\mathrm m}(t,X)=D_tf\bigl(t,\chi(t,X)\bigr)=\Bigl(\partial_tf+\nabla f\cdot u\Bigr)\bigl(t,\chi(t,X)\bigr),$$

with $D_t$ and the gradient of [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]. Writing
$\operatorname{div}(fu)=\nabla f\cdot u+f\operatorname{div}u$, the integrand
of (i) is $D_tf+f\operatorname{div}u$ at the corresponding current point.

The statement is conditional on the kinematic model and on the compact
containment $\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$; it asserts no conservation law, no
equation of motion and no empirical value.

items.title: The continuity equation of the continuum model: local form of mass balance, the material form, and the incompressibility reading
items.design_state: authored; step-1 readiness recorded in the batch notes
items.physical_scope: Conditional on the adopted mass-balance postulate, the smooth kinematic model and the Axiom of Countable Choice used by the transport machinery: conservation of the model mass of every material subregion is equivalent to the partial differential equation partial_t rho + div(rho u) = 0 on the current regions; equivalently the material derivative satisfies D_t rho = -rho div u, the product rho times the Jacobian is constant along each label worldline, the relative volume rate is div u, and the incompressibility condition div u = 0 is equivalent to the density being constant along each worldline in this branch. The theorem is a conditional model deduction and asserts no empirical value.

references.title: R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Section 4.2 (conservation of mass, local forms and the volumetric interpretation)
W. Barsukow, Introduction to Conservation Laws: Theory and Numerics (lecture notes, TUM, Winter term 2021/22), Section 1.1 (integral and differential forms of the continuity equation)
K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (September 1, 2026 complete volume), Section 8.3 (continuity equation and incompressibility of a continuum)

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(B,O,I)$ be body data
([[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]]), let $\chi$ be a motion of the model
with spatial velocity $u$ ([[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]],
[[def-cm-continuum-motion]]), let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with
$\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$, let $\Sigma$ be the swept region over
$\overline{J_0}$, and let $\rho:U\to(0,\infty)$ be a density field of class
$C^1$ on an open set $U$ containing $\Sigma$
([[def-cm17-density-and-mass]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).
Assume the mass-balance postulate (CM) of [[post-cm17-mass-balance]] for every
material subregion and every $t\in J_0$. Then:

**(i) Local form.** For every $(t,x)\in J_0\times\chi_t(B)$,

$$\partial_t\rho(t,x)+\operatorname{div}\bigl(\rho u\bigr)(t,x)=0 . \tag{C}$$

Conversely, if (C) holds on an open neighbourhood of $\Sigma$, then (CM)
holds for every material subregion and every $t\in J_0$.

**(ii) Material form.** On $J_0\times\chi_t(B)$ the material derivative of the
density satisfies

$$D_t\rho=-\rho\operatorname{div}u ,$$

and writing $J(t,X)=\det D_X\chi_t(X)$ along the motion, the product
$\rho\bigl(t,\chi(t,X)\bigr)J(t,X)$ is constant in $t$ for every label
$X\in B$.

**(iii) Volume rate.** For every $X\in B$ and $t\in J_0$ one has
$\partial_tJ(t,X)=J(t,X)\operatorname{div}u(t,\chi(t,X))$: the relative rate of
change of an infinitesimal material volume is $\operatorname{div}u$, and the
identity of (ii) is the statement that density times volume is conserved
along a label. In particular $\operatorname{div}u=0$ on the swept region if
and only if $\rho$ is constant along every label worldline ($D_t\rho=0$).

The statement is a conditional deduction from the adopted mass balance and
the kinematic model; it asserts no equation of motion, no constitutive
relation and no empirical value.

items.title: Traction fields and stress matrices of the continuum model, with units and sign conventions
items.design_state: authored; step-1 readiness recorded in the batch notes
items.physical_scope: The model's contact-force quantity: a traction field assigning to each point and unit normal the force per unit area exerted across a surface, its dimensions, and the stress matrix representing it when one exists; the sign convention identifying compressive normal traction with negative scalar stress, the component reading, and the distinction from body-force densities. Existence of a representing stress matrix, its continuity and its symmetry are not asserted here; they are conditional conclusions of the balance items of this page. No measured force is asserted.

references.title: R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Section 4.3 (force, Cauchy's hypothesis for contact forces, traction and the stress tensor)
K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (September 1, 2026 complete volume), Section 7.2 (the stress tensor and the force on a surface element)

items.statement:
Fix body data $(B,O,I)$ and a motion $\chi$ of the model with current regions
$\Omega_t=\chi_t(B)$, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ be an open
set containing the swept region over a compactly contained interval
([[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]], [[def-cm-continuum-motion]]). Let
$S^2=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:\|n\|_2=1\}$ be the unit sphere.

A **traction field of the model** is a map

$$t:U\times S^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,$$

read with the convention of [[def-cm-traction-and-stress]]: $t(s,x,n)$ is the
force per unit area exerted **by the material on the side towards which $n$
points upon the material on the other side**, at the point $x$ of a surface
whose unit normal is $n$, at time $s$. Its dimension is that of force per
area, $[t]=\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-2}$, read in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$
([[def-cm01-units]]).

A $C^1$ field of matrices $\sigma:U\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ **represents** the
traction field when

$$t(s,x,n)=\sigma(s,x)\,n\qquad\text{for every }(s,x,n)\in U\times S^2 ,$$

the product being matrix-vector multiplication. The existence of such a
$\sigma$ for a given traction field is **not asserted here**: it is a
conditional conclusion of the balance items of this page. When it exists,
$\sigma(s,x)$ is the **stress matrix** of the model at that event, and its
entries read $\sigma_{ij}=\bigl(t(s,x,e_j)\bigr)_i$: the $i$-th component of
the traction across the surface with normal $e_j$.

The isotropic matrix $-\lambda I_3$ with $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ represents the
**normal** traction $t(n)=-\lambda n$: under the convention above, positive
$\lambda$ is a compressive normal traction and $\lambda$ is called the
**pressure** in this sign convention, while $\sigma_{11}=\sigma_{22}
=\sigma_{33}=0$ and $\sigma_{12}=\sigma_{13}=\sigma_{23}=0$ describe a
pressure-free state. The **body-force density** is a separate object: a
continuous field $b$ with the dimension of acceleration, $[b]=\ell\tau^{-2}$,
whose force per unit volume is $\rho b$. A traction field need not satisfy
$t(-n)=-t(n)$ and its representing matrix, when one exists, need not be
symmetric; both properties are separate conditional conclusions.

items.title: Adopted force model of the continuum branch: continuous body forces and Cauchy contact tractions
items.design_state: authored; step-1 readiness recorded in the batch notes
items.physical_scope: Adoption of the force description of the continuum branch: a continuous body-force field per unit mass on the swept region and a continuous traction field, force per unit area, depending on a contact surface only through its unit normal at the point (Cauchy's hypothesis). The postulate excludes couple stresses, nonlocal contact interactions, curvature-dependent contact forces, and electromagnetic, thermal or chemical forces; it asserts no balance law, no constitutive relation and no measured value.

references.title: R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Section 4.3 (body forces, contact forces and Cauchy's hypothesis), Section 4.4 (the traction on a surface)
K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (September 1, 2026 complete volume), Section 7.2 (bulk and surface forces and the stress tensor)

items.statement:
Adopt for every model of the continuum kinematic branch
([[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]]) the following description of the
forces acting on the body, read in the fixed inertial frame and with the
dimensions of [[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]].

**(i) Body forces.** There is a continuous field
$b:U\to\mathbb R^3$ on an open set $U$ containing the swept region of the
motion over its time window, the **body force per unit mass**, of dimension
$[b]=\ell\tau^{-2}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). The body force exerted on an
admissible region $D$ is $\int_D\rho b\,dx$, of dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$
(force).

**(ii) Contact forces and Cauchy's hypothesis.** There is a traction field
$t:U\times S^2\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^1$, hence continuous, in the sense of
[[def-cm17-traction-and-stress]], force per unit area, with dimension
$[t]=\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-2}$. The definition of a traction field already
encodes **Cauchy's hypothesis**: the contact force exerted across a surface at
a point depends on the surface only through the value of its unit normal at
that point, so two surfaces through the same point with the same unit normal
experience the same traction. The contact force exerted across the boundary of
an admissible region $D$ is $\int_{\partial D}t(y,\nu_D(y))\,dS(y)$, with the
outward unit normal $\nu_D$ and the surface integral of the current-region
class. No dependence of $t$ on the curvature of the surface, on higher
derivatives of the surface, or on the distant shape of the body is introduced;
no surface couples, no traction singularities and no contact forces on curves
are introduced.

**(iii) Exclusions.** This force description is **not** adopted, and no
statement of this page covers: couple stresses or distributions of surface
couples; contact interactions that depend on the geometry of the surface
beyond its tangent plane at the point (thin boundary layers, capillarity at
contact lines, adhesion laws with curvature dependence); nonlocal contact
interactions; electromagnetic, thermal, chemical and radiative forces; and
body couples. A model with such features requires an extended force
description and its own balance laws.

**(iv) Status.** These are adopted assumptions about how forces are
represented in the model. No balance of forces is asserted by this postulate;
the balance principles are the subject of the next postulate, and the
existence of a representing stress matrix is a conditional conclusion of the
theorem that applies Cauchy's tetrahedron argument to those balances. The
fields $b$ and $t$ are model quantities; no measured force is asserted, and
the frame-covariance requirement of the kinematic branch applies to them.

items.title: Adopted balance principles of the continuum model: force and couple-free torque balance on every admissible region
items.design_state: authored; step-1 readiness recorded in the batch notes
items.physical_scope: Adoption of the balance principles of the continuum branch in force form: on every admissible bounded piecewise C-one region inside the current region, the surface traction resultant balances minus the volume integral of the body force minus the inertial term rho a, and the corresponding torque about any fixed origin balances likewise with no body or surface couples. The postulate excludes couple stresses, electromagnetic momentum exchange, mass sources and non-inertial frames; it asserts no constitutive law, no existence of a stress matrix and no measured value.

references.title: R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Sections 4.4-4.6 (balance of linear and angular momentum and the field equations)
K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (September 1, 2026 complete volume), Section 7.2 (Eq. (7.25) and the bulk-plus-surface force balance of a continuum element)

items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue volume and surface integration used in these general balances. The pointwise field and open-region predicates are unaffected.

Adopt for every model of the continuum branch, together with the force
description of [[post-cm17-contact-force-model]] and the fields of
[[def-cm17-density-and-mass]] and [[def-cm17-traction-and-stress]], the
following balance principles.

**(i) Setting.** Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ be an open set
containing the swept region of the motion over its time window. The density
$\rho$, the spatial velocity $u$ and the material acceleration $a=D_tu$ are
continuous on $U$ ([[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]],
[[def-cm-continuum-motion]]), and $b$ and $t$ are the body-force and traction
fields of [[post-cm17-contact-force-model]]. For $s$ in the time window the
current region is $\Omega_s=\chi_s(B)$.

**(ii) Admissible regions.** An **admissible region at time $s$** is a
bounded piecewise $C^1$ Euclidean domain with a specified finite presentation
with $D\subseteq\Omega_s$, whose closure lies in the open domain of the fields at time $s$
([[def-bounded-piecewise-c-one-euclidean-domain]]), with outward unit normal
$\nu_D$ off its edge set and boundary term the sum of the surface integrals
over its faces ([[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]).

**(iii) Balance of forces.** For every time $s$ and every admissible region
$D$ at time $s$,

$$\int_{\partial D}t\bigl(s,y,\nu_D(y)\bigr)\,dS(y)+\int_D\bigl(\rho b-\rho a\bigr)(s,y)\,dy=0 . \tag{F}$$

Read as a momentum balance, (F) says that the resultant contact force on $D$
equals $\int_D\rho a\,dy-\int_D\rho b\,dy$; equivalently contact plus body force equals $\int_D\rho a\,dy$, i.e. the total applied force
equals the mass times acceleration of the region, with the inertial term
written as a volume force.

**(iv) Balance of torques, with no couples.** For every time $s$, every
admissible region $D$ at time $s$, and every fixed origin $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$,

$$\int_{\partial D}(y-x_0)\times t\bigl(s,y,\nu_D(y)\bigr)\,dS(y)+\int_D(y-x_0)\times\bigl(\rho b-\rho a\bigr)(s,y)\,dy=0 , \tag{T}$$

the cross product being that of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]).
The balance is imposed with the **same** volume force density $\rho b-\rho a$
as in (F); there are no body couples and no surface couples. Since the
identity holds for every origin, the choice of $x_0$ is immaterial given (F).

**(v) Exclusions and status.** These principles are **not** adopted for: bodies
with couple stresses or surface couples; systems exchanging momentum with
electromagnetic or thermal fields (the momentum of those fields would have to
be accounted for separately); bodies with mass sources; and descriptions in
non-inertial frames (where additional inertial terms appear and are excluded
by the choice of the fixed inertial frame of
[[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]]). The principles are adopted model
assumptions, not derived here; comparisons of predicted motions with
observations can support them under stated apparatus assumptions, and no
measurement is asserted or used by this postulate. In particular, the
existence of a representing stress matrix, its continuity and its symmetry
are **not** assumed here; they are conditional conclusions of the theorem
items of this page, whose arguments apply the balance principles exactly as
stated.

items.title: Existence, uniqueness and symmetry of the stress matrix from the adopted balance principles
items.design_state: authored; step-1 readiness recorded in the batch notes
items.physical_scope: Conditional on the adopted force model and balance principles: on every bounded spatial region inside the current configuration the continuous traction field is represented by a unique continuous stress matrix, the reversed-normal identity t(-n) = -t(n) holds, and the couple-free torque balance forces the stress matrix to be symmetric. The result is a conditional deduction from the adopted balance principles and the cited mathematical Cauchy-tetrahedron and angular-balance theorems; it asserts no positivity, no constitutive relation and no measured stress.

references.title: R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Sections 4.3-4.5 (Cauchy's tetrahedron, existence of the stress tensor and symmetry from angular momentum)
K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (September 1, 2026 complete volume), Section 7.2 (the stress tensor, its symmetry from the torque balance, Eq. (7.25))

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the surface and divergence machinery of
the cited theorems. Let the model and its fields be as in
[[post-cm17-momentum-balance]]: a motion $\chi$ with current regions
$\Omega_s$, a continuous density field $\rho$, spatial velocity $u$ and
material acceleration $a=D_tu$, a continuous body-force field $b$ and a
continuous traction field $t$, with the balance principles (F) and (T) of
that postulate holding for every admissible region at every time $s$.

Then for every time $s$ and every bounded open set $W\subseteq\Omega_s$ with
$\overline W$ contained in the open domain of the fields at time $s$ there is
a unique continuous matrix field

$$\sigma(s,\cdot):W\longrightarrow M_3(\mathbb R)$$

such that

$$t(s,y,n)=\sigma(s,y)\,n\qquad\text{for every }(y,n)\in W\times S^2 ,$$

and necessarily

$$t(s,y,-n)=-t(s,y,n)\qquad\bigl((y,n)\in W\times S^2\bigr),\qquad \sigma(s,y)^{\mathsf T}=\sigma(s,y)\qquad(y\in W).$$

The stress matrix is continuous and unique per time; positivity of its
isotropic part, a constitutive relation and any measured stress are **not**
asserted.

items.title: The momentum equation of the continuum model: local form rho D_t u = rho b + div sigma
items.design_state: authored; step-1 readiness recorded in the batch notes
items.physical_scope: Conditional on the adopted mass-balance and momentum-balance postulates and on the Axiom of Countable Choice used by the transport and divergence machinery: the force-form balance on every admissible region, together with the continuity equation and the transport identity, is equivalent to the local momentum equation rho D_t u = rho b + div sigma on the current regions, where sigma is the stress matrix produced by the balance principles. The result is a conditional model deduction; it asserts no existence of solutions, no constitutive relation and no measured value.

references.title: R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Sections 4.4-4.6 (balance of momentum and the local field equations)
K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (September 1, 2026 complete volume), Section 7.2 (the key equation of continuum dynamics, Eq. (7.25))

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let the model of [[post-cm17-momentum-balance]] be
given with the mass-balance postulate of [[post-cm17-mass-balance]]: a motion
$\chi$ with spatial velocity $u$ and material acceleration $a=D_tu$
([[def-cm-continuum-motion]], [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]), a $C^1$
positive density field $\rho$ ([[def-cm17-density-and-mass]]), continuous
body forces and $C^1$ tractions ([[post-cm17-contact-force-model]]), and the
balance principles (F) and (T). Let $J_0\subseteq I$ have compact closure in
the time window. For localization, use the material subregions whose current images are bounded $C^1$ domains with closure in the open field domain ([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]), with boundary surface integral as in [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]; this class includes the inverse images of all sufficiently small current balls.

Let $\sigma$ be the stress matrix of
[[pthm-cm17-stress-matrix-and-symmetry]] on the current regions (whose
existence and symmetry follow from the same balance principles), and define
the row divergence

$$g_i:=\sum_{j=1}^{3}\partial_j\sigma_{ij}\qquad(i=1,2,3).$$

Then for every $(t,x)\in J_0\times\chi_t(B)$,

$$\rho(t,x)\,D_tu(t,x)=\rho(t,x)\,b(t,x)+g(t,x), \tag{M}$$

and for a symmetric $\sigma$ the row divergence $g$ coincides with the column
divergence, so (M) may be written $\rho D_tu=\rho b+\operatorname{div}\sigma$.
Conversely, with the same kinematics, positive density satisfying the continuity equation, and a $C^1$ symmetric stress representing the traction, (M) implies force balance (F) on every admissible region and integral momentum balance (L) on every admissible smooth material image. Thus these force and integral momentum formulations are equivalent to (M) under the stated regularity and continuity hypotheses. The statement is a conditional deduction from the adopted balances; it
asserts no solution existence, no boundary condition, no constitutive
relation and no empirical value.

items.title: Adopted isotropic linear elastic constitutive model with its small-strain regime and strain energy
items.design_state: authored; step-1 readiness recorded in the batch notes
items.physical_scope: Adoption of the small-strain isotropic linear elastic constitutive branch: displacement field, linear strain, stress matrix lambda (tr e) I + 2 mu_s e with positive-definite moduli, and the elastic strain-energy density with its positivity. The postulate states the small-strain kinematic idealization, the constancy of the reference density and the validity limits (small strains relative to a stress-free reference state, isothermal, no plasticity, viscosity, damage or coupling); it asserts no measured modulus, no boundary condition and no dynamical claim.

references.title: R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Section 11.2 and Problem 11.5 (linearized elasticity, isotropic stress-strain relations and the positive definite strain energy)
K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (September 1, 2026 complete volume), Section 7.3 (Hooke's law and the two elastic moduli of an isotropic medium)

items.statement:
Adopt the following constitutive model for the small-displacement elastic
branch of the continuum framework
([[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]],
[[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]]).

**(i) Small-displacement description.** There is a reference placement in
which the body is stress free and homogeneous, and the motion of the model is
described by a **displacement field** $\xi:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ of class
$C^2$ through $x(t,X)=X+\xi(t,X)$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]).
The model retains only the first-order term in the displacement gradient in
its strain measure: the **linear strain** is
$e=\tfrac12(D\xi+D\xi^{\mathsf T})$, equivalently
$e_{ij}=\tfrac12(\partial_j\xi_i+\partial_i\xi_j)$
([[def-cm-linear-elastic-constitutive-law]]). The displacement gradients are
assumed small in the sense of the model: the linear constitutive relation
below is used as the first-order approximation of the material response about
the stress-free reference state, and no quantitative strain threshold is
asserted by this postulate.

**(ii) Constitutive law.** The stress matrix of the branch is

$$\sigma=\lambda\,(\operatorname{tr}e)\,I_3+2\mu_s\,e ,$$

with **Lamé parameters** $\lambda,\mu_s\in\mathbb R$ satisfying the positivity
hypotheses $\mu_s>0$ and $\lambda+\tfrac{2\mu_s}{3}>0$
([[def-cm-linear-elastic-constitutive-law]]). Both parameters are constant in
space and time in this branch. Their dimension is that of stress,
$[\lambda]=[\mu_s]=\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-2}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]); in SI they are
measured in $\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$.

**(iii) Strain energy.** The **strain-energy density** of the branch is
$W(e)=\tfrac{\lambda}{2}(\operatorname{tr}e)^2+\mu_s\operatorname{tr}(e^2)$,
and under the positivity hypotheses of (ii) it satisfies $W(e)\ge0$ with
equality only for $e=0$ ([[lem-cm-isotropic-elastic-strain-energy-positivity]]).

**(iv) Density and kinematics.** In this branch the density is the constant
**reference density** $\rho_0>0$ of the homogeneous reference state; the
material acceleration is the second time derivative of the displacement,
$D_tu=\partial_t^2\xi$, and the spatial velocity is $u=\partial_t\xi$. These
replacements are part of the small-displacement idealization of the branch,
not consequences of the kinematic postulate
([[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]).

**(v) Validity, exclusions and status.** The branch is **not** adopted for:
finite strains where the displacement gradient is not small; anisotropic
materials (the law has two moduli and an isotropic form); plastic, viscous,
viscoelastic, damaged or fracturing response; temperature-dependent moduli or
thermoelastic coupling; and materials with internal structure. The Lamé
parameters are **material parameters**: whenever a numerical value of
$\lambda$ or $\mu_s$ is used in a deduction it enters as a measured empirical
premise with its own conditions and uncertainty, and no value is asserted
here. The constitutive law itself is adopted model structure, not a measured
law and not a consequence of the balance principles.

items.title: The displacement equation of the linear elastic branch: rho_0 partial_t^2 xi = rho_0 b + mu_s Laplacian xi + (lambda + mu_s) grad div xi
items.design_state: authored; step-1 readiness recorded in the batch notes
items.physical_scope: Conditional on the adopted mass and momentum balances and on the adopted small-strain isotropic linear elastic constitutive branch: in the material description of a small displacement field xi, the model's momentum equation is exactly rho_0 partial_t^2 xi = rho_0 b + mu_s Laplacian xi + (lambda + mu_s) grad div xi, with the second spatial derivatives of xi continuous and the material and spatial variables identified to first order as part of the branch's small-displacement idealization. The theorem is a conditional identity of the model; it asserts no solution existence, no error bound for the small-displacement replacement and no measured modulus.

references.title: R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Section 11.2 (the Navier equations of linearized elasticity)
K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (September 1, 2026 complete volume), Sections 7.3 and 7.7 (Hooke's law and the 3D elastic wave equation)

items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$
([[def-countable-choice]]) and the model of [[pthm-cm17-momentum-equation]]:
mass balance and the balance principles (F) and (T) of
[[post-cm17-momentum-balance]], with the stress matrix of
[[pthm-cm17-stress-matrix-and-symmetry]], so that the momentum equation

$$\rho\,D_tu=\rho\,b+\operatorname{div}\sigma \tag{M}$$

holds on the current regions. Suppose the model lies in the small-displacement
isotropic linear elastic branch of
[[post-cm17-linear-elastic-constitutive]]: the stress is
$\sigma=\lambda(\operatorname{tr}e)I_3+2\mu_s e$ with
$e=\tfrac12(D\xi+D\xi^{\mathsf T})$, the density is the constant reference
density $\rho_0>0$, the spatial velocity is $u=\partial_t\xi$ and the material
acceleration is $D_tu=\partial_t^2\xi$, where $\xi:I\times O\to\mathbb R^3$ is
of class $C^2$ with continuous second spatial derivatives and the material and
spatial variables are identified to first order as stated in that postulate.
Let $b$ be the body-force field of that model.

Then, with all derivatives taken in the spatial variables identified with the
material labels, the momentum equation (M) of the branch is equivalent to the
**displacement equation**

$$\rho_0\,\partial_t^2\xi=\rho_0\,b+\mu_s\,\Delta\xi+(\lambda+\mu_s)\,\nabla(\operatorname{div}\xi), \tag{E}$$

equivalently componentwise
$\rho_0\partial_t^2\xi_i=\rho_0b_i+\mu_s\Delta\xi_i+(\lambda+\mu_s)\partial_i(\operatorname{div}\xi)$
for $i=1,2,3$, where $\Delta=\sum_j\partial_j^2$ and
$\operatorname{div}\xi=\sum_j\partial_j\xi_j$
([[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]). In particular, for $b\equiv0$
equation (E) is linear with constant coefficients. The statement asserts no
solution existence, no boundary conditions and no measured modulus.

items.title: Plane elastic waves in the adopted model: the dispersion condition and the longitudinal and transverse speeds
items.design_state: authored; step-1 readiness recorded in the batch notes
items.physical_scope: Conditional on the small-strain isotropic linear elastic branch: a plane displacement wave a cos(<k,x> - omega t) satisfies the model's displacement equation with zero body force on all of space-time if and only if the dispersion relation rho_0 omega^2 a = mu_s |k|^2 a + (lambda + mu_s) <k,a> k holds; parallel amplitudes give the longitudinal speed root((lambda+2mu_s)/rho_0) and orthogonal amplitudes give the transverse speed root(mu_s/rho_0), both real and positive under the branch's positivity hypotheses. The theorem asserts no completeness of plane waves, no measured modulus and no empirical value.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (September 1, 2026 complete volume), Section 7.7 (plane longitudinal and transverse elastic waves and their speeds)
R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Section 11.2 (the isotropic linearized elastic field equations)

items.statement:
Adopt the small-displacement isotropic linear elastic branch of
[[post-cm17-linear-elastic-constitutive]] with reference density $\rho_0>0$
and Lamé parameters $\lambda,\mu_s$ satisfying $\mu_s>0$ and
$\lambda+\tfrac{2\mu_s}{3}>0$, and let (E) be the displacement equation of
[[pthm-cm17-linear-elastic-equation-of-motion]] with body force
$b\equiv0$. Let $k,a\in\mathbb R^3$ and $\omega\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$,
and define the **plane displacement wave**

$$\xi(t,x):=a\cos\bigl(\langle k,x\rangle_2-\omega t\bigr),$$

with the Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_2$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then $\xi$ satisfies (E) on all of
$\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ if and only if

$$\rho_0\omega^2a=\mu_s|k|_2^2\,a+(\lambda+\mu_s)\,\langle k,a\rangle_2\,k. \tag{D}$$

Consequently, for $a\ne0$: if $a$ is parallel to $k$ (**longitudinal**), then
$\rho_0\omega^2=(\lambda+2\mu_s)|k|_2^2$, and the squared speed
$c_L^2:=(\lambda+2\mu_s)/\rho_0$ is real and positive; if $a$ is orthogonal to
$k$ (**transverse**), then $\rho_0\omega^2=\mu_s|k|_2^2$, and
$c_T^2:=\mu_s/\rho_0$ is real and positive. Both $c_L$ and $c_T$ have the
dimension of velocity, $[c_L]=[c_T]=\ell\tau^{-1}$
([[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]], [[def-cm01-units]]). No assertion is
made that every solution of (E) is a superposition of plane waves, and no
measured modulus or speed is claimed.

items.title: Adopted fluid constitutive branches: incompressible Newtonian, barotropic inviscid, and the periodic-cell idealization
items.design_state: authored; step-1 readiness recorded in the batch notes
items.physical_scope: Adoption of the fluid constitutive branches of the continuum framework: an incompressible Newtonian model with constant density, divergence-free velocity, pressure and positive dynamic viscosity; a barotropic inviscid model with a pressure law, conservative body force and enthalpy; and the periodic-cell idealization on the three-torus used by the local well-posedness theorem. The postulate excludes compressible viscosity with thermal coupling, non-Newtonian and turbulent-closure models, surface tension and multiphase flow, and asserts no measured viscosity, pressure law or boundary condition.

references.title: R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Sections 12.1-12.3 (inviscid and incompressible viscous fluid models, with the Newtonian example)
K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (September 1, 2026 complete volume), Sections 8.4-8.5 (ideal and viscous incompressible fluid models)

items.statement:
Adopt the following constitutive branches for models of the continuum
framework ([[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]],
[[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]]), with the stress conventions of
[[def-cm17-traction-and-stress]].

**(a) Incompressible Newtonian fluid.** Model data are a constant density
$\rho>0$, a **dynamic viscosity** $\eta>0$ (constant, dimension
$\mu\ell^{-1}\tau^{-1}$, in SI measured in $\mathrm{Pa\,s}$,
[[def-cm01-units]]) and a pressure field $p$ of class $C^1$. The branch
consists of the **incompressibility constraint**

$$\operatorname{div}u=0$$

on the current regions ([[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]) together with
the **Newtonian stress field**

$$\sigma=-p\,I_3+\eta\bigl(Du+Du^{\mathsf T}\bigr),$$

the second term being symmetric. By the continuity equation of the model
([[pthm-cm17-continuity-equation]]) the constraint $\operatorname{div}u=0$ is
equivalent, in this branch, to the density being constant along every label
worldline, so the constant-density reading is consistent with the adopted mass
balance.

**(a0) Constant-density incompressible inviscid fluid.** Adopt separately the Euler branch: $\rho>0$ is constant, $\operatorname{div}u=0$, pressure is a Lagrange multiplier enforcing this constraint, and $\sigma=-pI_3$. This is the same stress form as (a) with $\eta=0$, adopted as model structure; it is not obtained by imposing a barotropic pressure law on a constant density. No positive-viscosity assumption is used in this branch.

**(b) Barotropic inviscid fluid.** Model data are a $C^1$ **pressure law**
$p:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ and a $C^1$ potential $V$ with the conservative
body force $b=-\nabla V$. The branch's stress field is
$\sigma=-p(\rho)I_3$, where $\rho$ is the model density field of
[[def-cm17-density-and-mass]]. Its **enthalpy** is the function
$h(r)=\int_{\rho_{\mathrm r}}^r p'(s)s^{-1}\,ds$, with a fixed model reference density $\rho_{\mathrm r}>0$ of the same density dimension as $r$, characterised by
$h'(\rho)=p'(\rho)/\rho$
([[def-cm-fluid-constitutive-models]]).

**(c) Periodic-cell idealization and scale conventions.** Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the normalized product measure and Fourier/Sobolev machinery of this clause; the pointwise stress laws of (a), (a0) and (b) do not use this premise. Fix a cell side length $L_*>0$ and velocity scale $U_*>0$ as model data with dimensions $\ell$ and $\ell\tau^{-1}$, and let $T_*=L_*/U_*$ be the time scale. The physical spatial cell is $(\mathbb R/L_*\mathbb Z)^3$, with physical volume $L_*^3$; it describes a spatially periodic ideal medium, not a material boundary or a measured wall law. Write $\tau=t/T_*$ and $y=x/L_*\in\mathbb T^3$, using an optional fixed time origin. For physical velocity $u_{\mathrm{phys}}$, pressure $P_{\mathrm m}$ and density $\rho$, define dimensionless fields and viscosity by
$$U(\tau,y)=\frac{u_{\mathrm{phys}}(T_*\tau,L_*y)}{U_*},\qquad \Pi(\tau,y)=\frac{P_{\mathrm m}(T_*\tau,L_*y)}{\rho U_*^2},\qquad \nu_*:=\frac{\eta}{\rho U_*L_*}.$$
The inviscid branch has $\eta=0$ and $\nu_*=0$. The normalized unit-torus measure and $H^s$ norms of [[def-periodic-vector-sobolev-space-and-leray-projection]] apply to $U$, not to an unscaled dimensionful velocity. In the absence of body force the physical equation scales exactly to
$$\partial_\tau U+(U\cdot\nabla_y)U=-\nabla_y\Pi+\nu_*\Delta_yU,\qquad \operatorname{div}_yU=0.$$
A dimensionless lifespan $T$ is a physical lifespan $T_*T$, and $P_{\mathrm m}=\rho U_*^2\Pi$. Pressure has zero spatial mean as the chosen gauge. The periodic geometry and the scales are adopted model data, not observed boundary behavior or measured parameters. A change of inertial frame carries the cell lattice to $R(L_*\mathbb Z^3)$; the unit-torus identification is made in the correspondingly rotated cell coordinates, rather than silently keeping a fixed lattice under an arbitrary rotation.

**(d) Validity and exclusions.** The branches are **not** adopted for:
compressible viscous flow with temperature dependence or thermal coupling;
non-Newtonian materials (shear-dependent or viscoelastic response); turbulent
closures or averaged models (whose additional terms are not the fields of
this branch); surface tension, capillarity and multiphase interfaces; and
flows in which the continuum description itself fails at the scales of
interest. Wall conditions such as the no-slip condition used later are
additional **ideal boundary data**; they are adopted where stated, not
derived, and their empirical validity has limits that are not formalized
here.

**(e) Status.** The constitutive laws, the incompressibility constraint, the
pressure law and the periodic-cell geometry are adopted model structure, not
consequences of the balance principles. The viscosity $\eta$, the pressure
law and the potential are **model parameters or model functions**: whenever
numerical values are used they enter as measured empirical premises with
their conditions and uncertainty, and no measured value is asserted by this
postulate.

items.title: Local existence, uniqueness and pressure reconstruction for the incompressible fluid model on the periodic cell
items.design_state: authored; step-1 readiness recorded in the batch notes
items.physical_scope: Conditional on the adopted incompressible Newtonian (or inviscid Euler) fluid branch and its periodic-cell idealization, and on the Axiom of Countable Choice used by the Fourier machinery: for smooth divergence-free periodic initial velocity data of finite H^s norm (integer s at least 4) there is a local time T depending only on that norm, and a smooth periodic velocity and a unique smooth mean-zero pressure satisfying the model's field equations exactly; the velocity is unique on the interval among smooth divergence-free solutions, depends continuously on initial data in H^{s-1}, and no all-time bound or global regularity conclusion is claimed. The theorem concerns the Eulerian field equations and does not construct the material label map; no measured viscosity or pressure is asserted.

references.title: R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Sections 12.2-12.3 (the incompressible viscous fluid equations and the inviscid limit)

K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (September 1, 2026 complete volume), Sections 8.4-8.5 (ideal and viscous incompressible fluid dynamics, with the Navier-Stokes equation and its exact channel solutions)

items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Adopt the constant-density incompressible Newtonian or inviscid branch and periodic-cell convention of [[post-cm17-fluid-constitutive]] clauses (a), (a0), (c), with $\rho>0$, $\eta\ge0$, and no body force. Fix the model scales $L_*,U_*>0$, $T_*=L_*/U_*$ and put $\nu_*:=\eta/(\rho U_*L_*)$. Let $s\ge4$ be an integer and $U_0$ a smooth divergence-free field on the dimensionless unit torus, with $Y_0:=\|U_0\|_{H^s}<\infty$. Set
$$T:=\begin{cases}(2C_sY_0)^{-1},&Y_0>0,\\1,&Y_0=0,\end{cases}$$
where $C_s$ is the constant used by [[thm-local-smooth-periodic-euler-viscous-solution]]. Then:

**(i) Reduction and physical-time conversion.** Under $\tau=t/T_*$, $y=x/L_*$ and the scaling of the postulate, the physical continuity and momentum equations with $\sigma=-P_{\mathrm m}I_3+\eta(D_xu_{\mathrm{phys}}+D_xu_{\mathrm{phys}}^{\mathsf T})$ are equivalent to
$$\partial_\tau U+(U\cdot\nabla_y)U=-\nabla_y\Pi+\nu_*\Delta_yU,\qquad \operatorname{div}_yU=0.$$
For smooth fields with zero-mean pressure, these are equivalent to
$$\partial_\tau U+P((U\cdot\nabla_y)U)=\nu_*\Delta_yU \tag{PE}$$
and the pressure reconstruction below. A solution on $[0,T]$ is a physical solution on $[0,T_*T]$.

**(ii) Existence and pressure.** There is $U\in C^\infty([0,T]\times\mathbb T^3;\mathbb R^3)$ with $U(0)=U_0$, $\operatorname{div}_yU=0$ and (PE), and $\sup_{[0,T]}\|U\|_{H^m}\le\|U_0\|_{H^m}e^{4C_mY_0T}$ for every $m\ge s$. There is a unique smooth dimensionless zero-mean pressure $\Pi$ giving the primitive equations in (i). The physical fields are
$$u_{\mathrm{phys}}(t,x)=U_*U(t/T_*,x/L_*),\qquad P_{\mathrm m}(t,x)=\rho U_*^2\Pi(t/T_*,x/L_*).$$
They satisfy the adopted field equations for both $\eta>0$ and the separately adopted $\eta=0$ Euler branch.

**(iii) Uniqueness and dependence on data.** Fix $B>0$. For all smooth divergence-free data $U_0,V_0$ with both $H^s$ norms at most $B$, the corresponding solutions exist on the common dimensionless interval $[0,T_B]$, $T_B=(2C_sB)^{-1}$, with $U(0)=U_0$ and $V(0)=V_0$. If $U_0=V_0$ then $U=V$. On this bounded data set the solution map is continuous from the $L^2$ topology into $C([0,T_B],H^{s-1})$, as in [[thm-fluid-uniqueness-and-continuous-dependence]]. The common physical interval is $[0,T_*T_B]$ for the same fixed scales and material parameters.

**(iv) Scope.** The Sobolev norm and $T,T_B$ are dimensionless; physical time also depends on the chosen scales. The theorem concerns smooth Eulerian fields on the adopted periodic cell. It constructs no material label map, no nonperiodic or rough-data solution and no global-in-time bound; no measured parameter is used.

items.title: The continuum string model as the proved limit of the mass-spring chain, with explicit convergence and dispersion error
items.design_state: authored; step-1 readiness recorded in the batch notes
items.physical_scope: Conditional on the adopted mass-spring chain with the stated mass and stiffness scaling: for every smooth periodic solution of the one-dimensional wave equation with speed c = square root of tension over linear density, the chain with node mass density-times-spacing and spring constant tension-over-spacing reproduces the sampled continuum motion with explicit uniform O(a^{3/2}) nodal error and O(a^2) interpolation error, and the chain's exact dispersion relation reduces to the continuum one with a fourth-order error in the spacing. The theorem justifies the string model as an approximation of the discrete mechanical model in this regime; it asserts no claim that the string model is exact for any material, and no measured constant.

references.title: I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09/8.309 Fall 2014 course text), Section 6.1 (the chain of masses and springs, its Lagrangian and the continuum limit)
K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (September 1, 2026 complete volume), Sections 6.2-6.5 (coupled oscillators, the discrete chain and its continuum/standing-wave limits)

items.statement:
Let $L>0$, let $\rho_\ell>0$ be a linear mass density and let $\tau_s>0$ be a
tension scale, both in the units of [[def-cm01-units]], and put
$c:=\sqrt{\tau_s/\rho_\ell}$, of dimension $[c]=\ell\tau^{-1}$
([[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]]). For an integer $N\ge2$ put
$a:=L/N$ and consider the cyclic spring chain of
[[def-cm-cyclic-spring-chain]] with parameter $c$ and spacing $a$,
equivalently the chain of $N$ nodes of mass $m=\rho_\ell a$ and spring
constant $k_s=\tau_s/a$; the two descriptions agree because
$c^2/a^2=k_s/m$. Let $[0,T_{\max}]$ be a compact time interval and let
$u:[0,T_{\max}]\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in $t$ and $C^4$ in $x$,
$L$-periodic in $x$, and satisfy

$$u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}\qquad\text{on }[0,T_{\max}]\times\mathbb R ,$$

with $M:=\sup|\partial_x^4u|<+\infty$ and $M_2:=\sup|\partial_x^2u|<+\infty$.
Let $q$ be the chain solution with the sampled initial data
$q_j(0)=u(0,ja)$, $q_j'(0)=u_t(0,ja)$, put $e_j(t):=q_j(t)-u(t,ja)$ and
$C:=c^2\sqrt L\,M/12$. Then:

**(i)** $q$ exists and is unique on $[0,T_{\max}]$, and for every
$t\in[0,T_{\max}]$

$$\|e(t)\|_a\le\frac{Ca^2t^2}{2},\qquad\|e'(t)\|_a\le Ca^2t,\qquad \max_j|e_j(t)|\le\frac{Ca^{3/2}t^2}{2},$$

in the discrete norm of [[def-cm-cyclic-spring-chain]]; consequently the
nodal displacements converge to the sampled continuum motion uniformly on
$[0,T_{\max}]$ as $a\to0$ with $L,T_{\max}$ fixed.

**(ii)** With $I_aq$ the piecewise-linear interpolation of the chain data on
the circle of circumference $L$,

$$\sup_{x\in[0,L]}|I_aq(t,x)-u(t,x)|\le\max_j|e_j(t)|+\frac{M_2a^2}{8}\qquad(0\le t\le T_{\max}),$$

so the interpolated chain displacement converges uniformly to the continuum
solution as $a\to0$.

**(iii)** For $A\ne0$ and cyclic wave numbers $\kappa Na\in2\pi\mathbb Z$, the travelling ansatz $q_j(t)=A\cos(\kappa ja-\omega t)$ solves the
chain equation if and only if $\omega^2=(4c^2/a^2)\sin^2(\kappa a/2)$, and for these solutions with
$|\kappa a|\le1$ one has $|\omega^2-c^2\kappa^2|\le c^2\kappa^4a^2/12$: the
continuum dispersion relation is the long-wave limit with an explicit
fourth-order error in the spacing.

The result justifies the continuum string model with speed $c$ as the proved
limit of the discrete mechanical chain in this regime; it asserts no
exactness of the string model for any material and no measured constant.

items.title: The string model: d'Alembert solutions, fixed-end modes and uniqueness for the adopted one-dimensional continuum
items.design_state: authored; step-1 readiness recorded in the batch notes
items.physical_scope: Conditional on the adopted one-dimensional string model with tension and linear density (wave speed c = square root of tension over linear density, justified by the chain limit) and on the small transverse displacement idealization: the d'Alembert formula gives the unique C^2 solution of the Cauchy problem on the line for C^2 initial displacement and C^1 initial velocity, and for smooth odd periodic data the fixed-end sine-series solution exists, is unique among C^2 solutions and carries an explicit tail bound. The theorem asserts no measured tension or density, no nonlinear or bending corrections and no validity of the string model for any particular material.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (September 1, 2026 complete volume), Section 6.5 (standing waves of a fixed-end string and the wave equation)
I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09/8.309 Fall 2014 course text), Section 6.1 (continuum limit of the chain and the wave equation)

items.statement:
Adopt the one-dimensional string model: a uniform string of length $L>0$
(fixed ends) or of infinite extent, with linear mass density $\rho_\ell>0$
and tension $\tau_s>0$, whose small transverse displacement
$u:I\times J\to\mathbb R$ (with $J=\mathbb R$ or $J=[0,L]$) satisfies

$$u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx},\qquad c:=\sqrt{\tau_s/\rho_\ell},$$

where the identification of $c$ with the chain limit is that of
[[pthm-cm17-chain-limit-of-the-string-model]] and the dimensions are those of
[[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]], [[def-cm01-units]]. Then:

**(i) Cauchy problem on the line.** For $f\in C^2(\mathbb R)$ and
$g\in C^1(\mathbb R)$ the function

$$u(t,x):=\frac{f(x-ct)+f(x+ct)}{2}+\frac{1}{2c}\int_{x-ct}^{x+ct}g(s)\,ds$$

is of class $C^2$ on $\mathbb R^2$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), satisfies $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$
with $u(0,\cdot)=f$ and $u_t(0,\cdot)=g$, and is the unique $C^2$ field on
$\mathbb R^2$ with those data.

**(ii) Fixed ends.** Let $F$ be odd and $2L$-periodic of class $C^5$ and let
$G$ be odd and $2L$-periodic of class $C^4$
([[def-cm-sine-coefficients-of-periodic-functions]]) with finite
$M_5=\sup|F^{(5)}|$, $M_4=\sup|G^{(4)}|$. Then the sine series $u$ of the
smooth string theorem exists with absolutely and uniformly convergent
termwise derivatives up to second order, satisfies $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$,
$u(t,0)=u(t,L)=0$, $u(0,\cdot)=F|_{[0,L]}$, $u_t(0,\cdot)=G|_{[0,L]}$, is the
unique $C^2$ solution on $[0,T]\times[0,L]$ of that boundary-value problem,
and for every $N\ge1$ satisfies the tail bound
$|u-S_Nu|\le C(N+1)^{-4}$ with $C=2\bigl(2L^5M_5/\pi^5+2L^5M_4/(c\pi^5)\bigr)$
on $[-T,T]\times[0,L]$, where $S_Nu$ is the $N$-th partial sum of the series.

**(iii) Reading and scope.** The initial functions $f,g$ or $F,G$ are the
model's initial transverse displacement and velocity; the solutions are exact
for the model and are not approximations within it. The model is the linear
small-transverse-displacement idealization of the string: bending stiffness,
longitudinal motion, external forcing and large-amplitude geometric
nonlinearity are excluded, and no measured tension, density or displacement
is asserted.

items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the cited Lebesgue transport and continuity suppliers.

Let $L_0>0$ have dimension length and let $B=(0,L_0)^3\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be the reference cube (the unit-cube case is $L_0=1\,\mathrm m$). Fix an expansion rate $\alpha>0$ with $[\alpha]=\tau^{-1}$ and put $I=(-1/\alpha,\infty)$ and define the uniform
expansion

$$\chi(t,X):=\bigl((1+\alpha t)X_1,(1+\alpha t)X_2,(1+\alpha t)X_3\bigr)\qquad\bigl((t,X)\in I\times\mathbb R^3\bigr).$$

Then $\chi$ is a motion of $B$ on $I$ in the sense of
[[def-cm-continuum-motion]] (with $O=\mathbb R^3$): it is $C^\infty$, each
$\chi_t$ is a diffeomorphism with $D_X\chi_t=(1+\alpha t)I_3$ and
$J(t,X)=(1+\alpha t)^3>0$ on $I\times B$. Adopt the model of
[[post-cm17-continuum-kinematic-model]] with these data and the
constant-reference-density field

$$\rho(t,x):=\frac{\rho_0}{(1+\alpha t)^3}\qquad(\rho_0>0)$$

on the swept region. Then:

1. the spatial velocity is $u(t,x)=\alpha x/(1+\alpha t)$ and
   $\operatorname{div}u(t,x)=3\alpha/(1+\alpha t)$
   ([[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]);
2. the model mass of $B$ at time $t$ is
   $\int_{\chi_t(B)}\rho\,dx=\rho_0L_0^3$ for every $t\in I$: the mass-balance
   assumption of [[post-cm17-mass-balance]] holds for every material subregion, since more generally $m(t,B')=\rho_0\operatorname{vol}(B')$, and the continuity
   equation $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$ of
   [[pthm-cm17-continuity-equation]] holds identically on $I\times\mathbb R^3$;
3. for the field $f(t,x):=x_1^2$ the transport identity of
   [[pthm-cm17-transport-and-material-derivative]] is verified exactly:
   with $F(t)=\int_{\chi_t(B)}f(t,x)\,dx$ one has $F(t)=L_0^5(1+\alpha t)^5/3$ and
   $F'(t)=5\alpha L_0^5(1+\alpha t)^4/3=\int_{\chi_t(B)}(\partial_tf+\operatorname{div}(fu))\,dx$
   for every $t\in I$;
4. along each label the density satisfies
   $\rho(t,\chi(t,X))(1+\alpha t)^3=\rho_0$, the constant-product form of density
   times volume of part (ii) of the continuity theorem, and the material
   derivative is
   $D_t\rho(t,\chi(t,X))=-3\alpha\rho_0/(1+\alpha t)^4=-\rho\operatorname{div}u$, as the
   material form of that theorem requires.

items.statement:
Adopt the isotropic linear elastic branch of
[[post-cm17-linear-elastic-constitutive]] with reference density
$\rho_0>0$ and moduli $\lambda,\mu_s$ with $\mu_s>0$ and
$\lambda+\tfrac{2\mu_s}{3}>0$, and let

$$c_L:=\sqrt{\frac{\lambda+2\mu_s}{\rho_0}},\qquad \xi(t,x):=A\cos\bigl(\kappa x_1-\omega t\bigr)\,e_1,\qquad \omega:=\kappa c_L,$$

with $A\ne0$, $\kappa\ne0$ and $e_1$ the first standard basis vector: a
longitudinal plane wave travelling along $e_1$. Then:

1. the linear strain is $e_{11}(t,x)=-A\kappa\sin(\kappa x_1-\omega t)$ with
   all other entries zero, so $\operatorname{tr}e=e_{11}$ and
   $e_0=e-\tfrac13(\operatorname{tr}e)I_3$ has Frobenius squared norm
   $\tfrac23e_{11}^2$;
2. the stress matrix is
   $$\sigma(t,x)=(\lambda+2\mu_s)e_{11}(t,x)\,e_1e_1^{\mathsf T}+\lambda e_{11}(t,x)\,(e_2e_2^{\mathsf T}+e_3e_3^{\mathsf T});$$
3. the displacement equation (E) of
   [[pthm-cm17-linear-elastic-equation-of-motion]] with $b\equiv0$ holds
   exactly: $\rho_0\partial_t^2\xi_1=(\lambda+2\mu_s)\partial_1^2\xi_1$;
4. the strain-energy density is
   $W(e)=(\tfrac\lambda2+\mu_s)e_{11}^2=\mu_s\tfrac23e_{11}^2
   +(\tfrac\lambda2+\tfrac{\mu_s}3)e_{11}^2\ge0$, with equality only where
   $e_{11}=0$; both coefficients in the decomposition are positive under the
   branch's hypotheses, and the squared speed
   $c_L^2=(\lambda+2\mu_s)/\rho_0$ is positive with $[c_L]=\ell\tau^{-1}$.

The example is an exact conditional computation within the linear string model and reports no measurement.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (September 1, 2026 complete volume), Section 6.5 (standing waves of the fixed-end string and the mode frequencies)
R. Laugesen, Harmonic Analysis Lecture Notes (arXiv:0903.3845), Chapters 1-2 (Fourier coefficients, uniqueness and summability of the sine series)

items.statement:
Let $L>0$, $c>0$ and $\beta\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and consider the
fixed-end string model of [[pthm-cm17-string-wave-solutions]] with initial
displacement and velocity

$$F(x):=\sin\Bigl(\frac{\pi x}{L}\Bigr)+\beta\sin\Bigl(\frac{3\pi x}{L}\Bigr),\qquad G(x):=0 .$$

Then $F$ is odd and $2L$-periodic of class $C^\infty$ and $G$ is odd and
$2L$-periodic of class $C^4$, with
$M_4=\sup|G^{(4)}|=0$ and
$M_5=\sup|F^{(5)}|\le(\pi/L)^5(1+243|\beta|)=:\overline M_5$
([[def-cm-sine-coefficients-of-periodic-functions]]). Put
$\omega_n:=n\pi c/L$ and

$$u(t,x):=\cos(\omega_1t)\sin\Bigl(\frac{\pi x}{L}\Bigr) +\beta\cos(\omega_3t)\sin\Bigl(\frac{3\pi x}{L}\Bigr).$$

Then:

1. the sine coefficients of $F$ are $b_1(F)=1$, $b_3(F)=\beta$ and $b_n(F)=0$
   otherwise, and the coefficients of $G$ all vanish; hence the series
   solution of [[thm-cm-smooth-string-fourier-series-solution]] is exactly
   the displayed finite sum $u$;
2. $u$ is $C^\infty$ on $\mathbb R^2$, satisfies $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$,
   vanishes at $x=0$ and $x=L$ for every $t$, and has
   $u(0,\cdot)=F$, $u_t(0,\cdot)=0$; by the uniqueness clause of the theorem
   it is the unique $C^2$ fixed-end solution with these data;
3. the d'Alembert formula of [[thm-cm-dalembert-formula-and-string-solutions]]
   with data $(F,0)$ gives the same field:
   $\tfrac12[F(x-ct)+F(x+ct)]=u(t,x)$ by the product-to-sum identity
   ([[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]],
   [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]]);
4. the tail bound at $N=1$ is verified: with
   $S_1u=\cos(\omega_1t)\sin(\pi x/L)$ one has
   $|u-S_1u|=|\beta||\cos(\omega_3t)||\sin(3\pi x/L)|\le|\beta|$, while the
   theorem gives $|u-S_Nu|\le C(N+1)^{-4}$ with
   $C\le\overline C:=4(1+243|\beta|)$, so the explicit upper estimate is
   $(1+243|\beta|)/4$ at $N=1$, which also dominates the direct bound
   $|\beta|$ for every $\beta$;
5. the mode frequencies satisfy $[\omega_n]=\tau^{-1}$ under
   $[c]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $[L]=\ell$ ([[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]]).
