K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (September 1, 2026 complete volume), Sections 6.2-6.5 (the discrete chain, its dispersion and its continuum limit)

items.statement:
Take the periodic string model of [[pthm-cm17-chain-limit-of-the-string-model]]
with circumference $L=2\pi$ and speed $c=1$ (that is, linear density
$\rho_\ell>0$ and tension $\tau_s=\rho_\ell$ in the units of
[[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]]), and the exact travelling-standing
solution

$$u(t,x):=A\sin x\cos t\qquad(A>0),$$

which is $2\pi$-periodic and solves $u_{tt}=u_{xx}$. For $N\ge2$ put
$a=2\pi/N$ and consider the cyclic spring chain of
[[def-cm-cyclic-spring-chain]] with parameter $c=1$ and spacing $a$, i.e.
node mass $m=\rho_\ell a$ and spring constant $k_s=\tau_s/a$. Then:

1. $M=\sup|\partial_x^4u|=A$, $M_2=\sup|\partial_x^2u|=A$ and the theorem's
   constant is $C=\sqrt{2\pi}A/12\approx0.20889A$;
2. the exact chain solution with the sampled data is
   $q_j(t)=A\sin(ja)\cos(\omega_at)$ with
   $\omega_a=2\sin(a/2)/a$ (positive for $0<a<\pi$), the exact nodal error is
   $e_j(t)=A\sin(ja)[\cos(\omega_at)-\cos t]$, and the theorem's bounds read
   $\|e(t)\|_a\le Ca^2t^2/2$,
   $\max_j|e_j(t)|\le \tfrac12Ca^{3/2}t^2$ and
   $\sup_x|I_aq-u|\le\max_j|e_j|+Aa^2/8$;
3. at $N=100$ (so $a=2\pi/100\approx0.062832$) and $t=1$ the evaluated bounds
   are $\|e(1)\|_a\le0.0004124A$,
   $\max_j|e_j(1)|\le0.001645A$ and
   $\sup|I_aq-u|\le0.002139A$, while the exact error satisfies
   $|e_j(1)|\le A|\omega_a-1|\approx0.00016447A$, so the theoretical bound is
   verified and visibly conservative;
4. the exact dispersion relation is
   $\omega_a^2=(4/a^2)\sin^2(a/2)$, and the theorem's bound
   $|\omega_a^2-1|\le a^2/12$ gives $\le0.00032899$ at $N=100$, while the
   exact value satisfies $|\omega_a^2-1|\approx0.00032899$.

items.title: A Riemann shock and a rarefaction of the scalar model: explicit weak solutions, entropy coefficients and initial trace
items.reference: batch-33 B page; constructed from the A-page statements
items.design_state: authored; step-1 readiness recorded in the batch notes
items.physical_scope: A worked scalar-model example of shock and rarefaction weak solutions: the Riemann data 2 and 1 with the entropy coefficients of the shock computed on the interval (1,2), and the rarefaction fan of the data 1 and 2 checked for continuity, the classical equation inside the fan and convergence of the initial trace. The scalar conservation law u_t + (u^2/2)_x = 0 is read as an idealized one-dimensional transport/compressible model; the example asserts no derivation of it from three-dimensional fluid mechanics and reports no measurement.

references.title: W. Barsukow, Introduction to Conservation Laws: Theory and Numerics (lecture notes, TUM, Winter term 2021/22), Chapters 2-5 (weak solutions, entropy conditions, Rankine-Hugoniot conditions and the scalar Riemann problem)

L. C. Evans, Entropy and Partial Differential Equations (UC Berkeley lecture notes, 2001), Chapter V (conservation laws: weak solutions, entropy conditions and the Rankine-Hugoniot condition for scalar laws)

items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the cited Lebesgue weak/entropy formulation.

Let $F(u)=\tfrac12u^2$ and use the weak and entropy formulations of
[[def-cm-scalar-conservation-law-weak-and-entropy-solution]], with the scalar
field $u$ read as the idealized one-dimensional model variable (a rescaled
density or transport quantity of the scalar model; see the remarks). Then:

1. **(Shock.)** For the Riemann data $u_L=2$, $u_R=1$ the piecewise constant
   field $u(t,x)=2$ for $x<\tfrac32t$ and $u(t,x)=1$ for $x>\tfrac32t$
   $(t>0)$, taking the right-state value on the shock line, is a weak solution of $u_t+(F(u))_x=0$: its interface residual is
   $-s[u]+[F(u)]=-\tfrac32\cdot(1-2)+\tfrac12(1^2-2^2)=\tfrac32-\tfrac32=0$
   with $s=\tfrac32$, so the weak identity (W) is satisfied for every test
   function by the split integration over the two half-planes.
2. **(Entropy of the shock.)** For every $k\in(1,2)$ the interface
   coefficient of the pair $(\eta_k,q_k)=(\lvert u-k\rvert,
   \operatorname{sign}(u-k)(u^2-k^2)/2)$ is
   $s[\eta_k]-[q_k]=-(k-2)(k-1)=(2-k)(k-1)>0$, so the shock satisfies the
   entropy inequality with strictly positive interface production on this range of $k$; the integrated inequality is strict only for nonnegative tests with $\int_0^\infty\varphi(t,st)dt>0$; for $k\notin[1,2]$ the
   coefficient vanishes and the inequality holds with equality.
3. **(Rarefaction.)** For the Riemann data $u_L=1$, $u_R=2$ the field
   $u(t,x)=1$ for $x\le t$, $u(t,x)=x/t$ for $t<x<2t$ and $u(t,x)=2$ for
   $x\ge2t$ $(t>0)$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$, satisfies
   $u_t+(F(u))_x=0$ classically inside the fan, and has initial trace $f$:
   $\int_{\mathbb R}\lvert u(t,x)-f(x)\rvert\,dx\le\tfrac32t\to0$ as
   $t\downarrow0$.
4. **(Weak kinks are unavoidable here.)** The shock profile is discontinuous
   across $x=\tfrac32t$ and the rarefaction is not differentiable across
   $x=t$ and $x=2t$; the classical derivation of the transport and balance
   identities of the continuum page does not apply at such sets, which is
   exactly why the weak formulation of the model is used. The admissibility
   of the shock and the equality case of the rarefaction are those of
   [[thm-cm-burgers-riemann-shock-and-rarefaction]].

items.title: Poiseuille and Couette channel flows of the viscous branch: explicit profiles, flux and wall data
items.reference: batch-33 B page; constructed from the A-page statements
items.design_state: authored; step-1 readiness recorded in the batch notes
items.physical_scope: A worked steady plane channel problem of the adopted incompressible Newtonian branch: the Poiseuille profile with pressure gradient 6, height 2 and viscosity 3 is verified against the model's momentum equation with zero body force, its flux per unit width 4/3 and centre speed 1 are computed, the Couette profile is verified with its nonzero curl, and the no-slip wall conditions are recorded as adopted ideal boundary data. The example reports no measurement.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (September 1, 2026 complete volume), Section 8.5 (Couette and Poiseuille flows with no-slip conditions)
R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Problems 12.9 and 12.14 (channel flows of the incompressible viscous model)

items.statement:
Adopt the incompressible Newtonian branch of [[post-cm17-fluid-constitutive]]
with constant density $\rho>0$, dynamic viscosity $\eta=3\,\mathrm{Pa\,s}$ and channel height $h=2\,\mathrm m$, whose SI coordinate domain is $O=\mathbb R\times(0,2)\times\mathbb R$ with
coordinates $(x,y,z)$, in the steady description and with no body force, and explicitly adopt the steady incompressible model equation
$\rho(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\nabla p+\eta\Delta u$ together with
$\operatorname{div}u=0$ ([[def-cm-fluid-constitutive-models]]). Here displayed coordinate profiles and numbers are SI numerical values: $v$ has units $\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, the flux per width has units $\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, $x,y,z$ are in metres and $p$ is in pascals. Deriving the adopted differential equation from integral balances would additionally require the mass and force premises of [[pthm-cm17-momentum-equation]]; those are not inferred from a constitutive law alone. Then:

1. **(Poiseuille.)** With pressure gradient $G=6\,\mathrm{Pa\,m^{-1}}$, i.e.
   $p(x)=p_0-6x$, the profile
   $u=(v(y),0,0)$, $v(y)=y(2-y)$ (the value $Gy(h-y)/(2\eta)$ of the general
   formula with $h=2,\eta=3$) satisfies $\operatorname{div}u=0$ and
   $\eta v''(y)=-6=-G$, hence the steady momentum equation with no body
   force; it satisfies the no-slip data $v(0)=v(2)=0$; its flux per unit
   width is $\int_0^2v(y)\,dy=4/3$ and its centre speed is $v(1)=1$.
2. **(Couette.)** With constant pressure and wall speed $V=2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, the profile
   $v(y)=Vy/2=y$ satisfies the same equations with zero body force and the
   boundary data $v(0)=0$, $v(2)=2$; its velocity gradient
   $D u=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&0\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}$ is not symmetric, so
   the flow is not irrotational: $\operatorname{curl}u=(0,0,-V/h)=(0,0,-1)$.
3. **(Uniqueness in the ansatz.)** Within the ansatz
   $u=(v(y),0,0)$, $p=p_0-Gx$, the difference of two profiles with the same
   $G$ and the same no-slip data satisfies $w''=0$ with $w(0)=w(2)=0$, hence
   $w\equiv0$: the Poiseuille profile is the unique steady solution in this
   class with those data.
4. **(Reading.)** The wall conditions are **adopted ideal boundary data**:
   the model is used with the no-slip assumption $v=0$ at the fixed walls,
   which is the idealization recorded in [[post-cm17-fluid-constitutive]];
   the profiles are exact solutions of the model and are not approximations
   within it. Dimensions: $[G]=\mu\ell^{-2}\tau^{-2}$, so
   $[Gh^3/\eta]=\ell^2\tau^{-1}$ (flux per unit width) and
   $[Gh^2/\eta]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ (speed), consistently with
   [[def-cm17-continuum-body-and-units]], [[def-cm01-units]].

items.title: Periodic shear fields: an exact steady Euler solution, failure for the viscous branch, and the classification of steady periodic shears
items.reference: batch-33 B page; constructed from the A-page statements
items.design_state: authored; step-1 readiness recorded in the batch notes
items.physical_scope: Worked checks on the periodic cell of the adopted fluid branch: the sinusoidal shear is verified to be an exact steady solution of the inviscid (Euler) branch with zero pressure and to fail the local existence theorem's projected equation for the viscous branch, and the steady periodic shear fields of the viscous branch with no body force are classified: only constants survive. The example uses the periodic-cell idealization and reports no measurement.

references.title: R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Section 12.3 (incompressible inviscid fluid and simple exact solutions)
K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (September 1, 2026 complete volume), Sections 8.4-8.5 (ideal fluid solutions and viscous shear flows)

items.statement:
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the cited periodic Sobolev and local-evolution suppliers.

Use the dimensionless variables of [[post-cm17-fluid-constitutive]] clause (c): $t,x,u$ in this example denote the scaled time, unit-torus position and velocity, $\nu=\eta/(\rho U_*L_*)$, and $p=P_{\mathrm m}/(\rho U_*^2)$. The physical fields are restored by $u_{\mathrm{phys}}=U_*u(t/T_*,x/L_*)$, $P_{\mathrm m}=\rho U_*^2p(t/T_*,x/L_*)$. Work on the periodic cell $\mathbb T^3=(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z)^3$ of
[[post-cm17-fluid-constitutive]] clause (c), with constant density $\rho>0$,
no body force and the stress of the branch. Let $A>0$, $\varphi\in\mathbb R$
and

$$u(t,x):=\bigl(A\sin(2\pi x_2+\varphi),0,0\bigr).$$

Then:

1. $\operatorname{div}u=0$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=0$, so with $p\equiv0$ the
   field is an exact steady solution of the **Euler** branch ($\nu=0$) of the
   model on the periodic cell: $\partial_tu+P((u\cdot\nabla)u)=\nu\Delta u$
   holds as $0=0$, and the primitive equation
   $\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u=-\nabla p+\nu\Delta u$ holds with $p\equiv0$;
2. the field satisfies the hypotheses of
   [[pthm-cm17-incompressible-periodic-local-evolution]]: it is smooth,
   divergence-free, periodic and has finite $H^s$ norm ($s\ge4$), and the
   displayed global solution is consistent with the local
   existence-uniqueness statement;
3. for the **viscous** branch ($\nu>0$) the field is **not** a solution:
   $\Delta u=-(2\pi)^2u\ne0$ and $P\Delta u=\Delta u$ because $u$ is
   divergence-free, so the projected equation would require
   $-\nu\cdot(2\pi)^2u=0$, which fails for $A>0$;
4. more generally, every steady periodic shear $u=(v(x_2),0,0)$ of the
   viscous branch with no body force and constant density is **constant**:
   the dimensionless equations force $\nabla p=\nu(v''(x_2),0,0)$, and periodicity
   of $p$ in $x_1$ together with periodicity of $v$ in $x_2$ forces
   $v''\equiv0$ and then $v\equiv\mathrm{const}$.

items.title: FALSE: the reversed-normal convention alone makes a continuous traction field a stress matrix. The field t(n)=|n_1|n refutes it
items.reference: batch-33 B page; constructed from the A-page statements
items.design_state: authored; step-1 readiness recorded in the batch notes

references.title: R. Abeyaratne, Continuum Mechanics, Volume II of Lecture Notes on the Mechanics of Solids (MIT, 1988, revised 2020), Section 4.3 (Cauchy's hypothesis and the need for force balance in the tetrahedron argument)
MIT OpenCourseWare 12.005, Applications of Continuum Mechanics, Lecture 3 (Cauchy tetrahedron and Cauchy's formula t = sigma n)

items.statement:
The false statement is: *every continuous traction field
$t:S^2\to\mathbb R^3$ satisfying the reversed-normal convention
$t(-n)=-t(n)$ for every $n\in S^2$ is represented by a matrix
$\sigma\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ with $t(n)=\sigma n$ for every $n$.*

The field constructed below is continuous and satisfies the convention, and
inherits Cauchy's hypothesis (it depends on the surface only through the unit
normal), but no matrix represents it. The refutation shows that the balance
hypothesis of the Cauchy-tetrahedron theorem is essential: symmetry of the
traction in the normal alone is not enough.
